author: high5
claim: Subgoal solved: every longest trail in G is closed.
evidence: Let T=(v_0,e_1,v_1,...,e_m,v_m) be a longest trail, and let H consist of its used edges. If v_m≠v_0, then at v_m all used-edge incidences arising from intermediate visits pair as arrival/departure pairs, while the final arrival is unpaired; loops contribute two incidences and preserve parity. Thus deg_H(v_m) is odd. No unused edge is incident with v_m, or it could be appended to T. Hence deg_G(v_m)=deg_H(v_m), contradicting the evenness of deg_G(v_m). Thus v_m=v_0.

author: high5
claim: Subgoal solved: a longest closed trail in connected G contains every edge.
evidence: Let T be a closed trail and S its vertices. If an omitted edge has an endpoint in S, select it. Otherwise choose an endpoint y of an omitted edge outside S; connectedness gives a path from S to y, and the first edge on that path leaving S is omitted and incident with S. Thus an omitted edge f has an endpoint w on T. Rotate the closed vertex-edge sequence of T to start and end at an occurrence of w and append f. This is a trail with one more edge, contradicting longestness. Therefore no edge is omitted.

author: high6
claim: Solved direct-longest-trail plan: Let (G) be a finite connected undirected graph with at least one edge. Suppose every vertex of (G) has even degree. Then (G) has a closed trail that traverses every edge exactly once.
evidence: Choose a trail T=(v_0,e_1,v_1,...,e_m,v_m) with the largest possible number m of edges; it exists because G is finite, and m>=1 because G has an edge. First T is closed. If v_0!=v_m, let A count arrivals at v_m and D count departures from v_m in T. Then A=D+1, while the number of incidences at v_m among the used edges is A+D=2D+1. Thus the used edges give odd degree at v_m. Since deg_G(v_m) is even, an edge incident with v_m is unused, and appending it extends T, contradiction. Hence v_0=v_m. Now suppose an edge is unused, and let w be one of its endpoints. Put S={v_0,...,v_m}. If w lies in S, that unused edge is incident with S. If w does not lie in S, connectedness gives a path from a vertex of S to w; the first edge on this path that leaves S is unused because every used edge has both endpoints in S. Thus in all cases there is an unused edge f incident with some x=v_j in S. Since T is closed, cyclically rotate its vertex-edge sequence to start and finish at x, preserving the fact that it is a trail and its used edge set. Append f. This gives a trail with m+1 edges, contradicting the choice of T. Hence no edge is unused. Since T is a trail, no edge repeats, so it traverses every edge exactly once; since it is closed, it is the required closed trail. author: high2
claim: Solved subgoal: an edge-maximal trail in an even-degree finite graph is closed.
evidence: Let the trail start at a and end at b. If a and b differ, the used incidences at b are odd: every visit before the final one has paired entry and exit incidences, and the final entry is unpaired. The total number of incidences at b is even, so the unused number is a nonnegative odd integer and therefore positive. An unused incident edge extends the trail, contradicting edge-maximality. Hence b=a.

links.attempt_summary: Endpoint incidence parity contradicts maximality unless the endpoints coincide.

author: high2
claim: Solved subgoal: deleting all edges of a closed trail from an even-degree graph leaves even degree at every vertex.
evidence: At each vertex of a closed trail, every arrival incidence is paired with the next departure incidence, including across the cyclic junction between the end and beginning. Thus the closed trail uses an even number of incidences at each vertex. Each original degree is even, so subtracting the used even number leaves an even residual degree.

author: high2
claim: Solved subgoal: a nonempty residual closed trail based at a current-trail vertex can be spliced into the current trail, and finitely many such splices exhaust all edges.
evidence: Rotate the cyclic representation of the current closed trail so it begins and ends at the attachment vertex w. Follow the residual closed trail from w back to w and then the rotated current trail. The two edge sets are disjoint, so their concatenation is a closed trail using each edge in their union once. The residual trail is nonempty, so each splice strictly increases the number of used edges; the finite edge set permits only finitely many splices. If any edge remained, the access and closure subgoals would permit another splice, so termination occurs only after all edges are used.

links.attempt_summary: Concatenate at the common vertex; disjointness preserves the trail property and finiteness forces exhaustion.

author: high4
claim: Subgoal solved: a maximal trail begun at a positive-degree vertex of a finite even-degree graph is a nonempty closed trail.
evidence: Choose, among all trails starting at s, one T having the largest number of edges; finiteness guarantees a choice, and positive degree makes T nonempty. If its endpoint t is not s, internal visits of T to t use edge-incidences in pairs while the final arrival uses one additional incidence. Hence T uses an odd number of incidences at t. Since the degree of t is even, at least one incident edge is not in T. Appending that edge gives a longer trail from s, a contradiction. Thus t=s and T is closed.

glossary.T: a longest trail starting at s

author: high4
claim: Subgoal solved: an edge-maximal closed trail in the target graph contains every edge.
evidence: Let C be an edge-maximal closed trail. If an edge is unused, connectedness yields a vertex w of C incident to an unused edge: if an endpoint is outside C, take the first vertex of C on a path from that endpoint to C; the entering path edge is unused because a used edge of C has both endpoints on C. Delete the edges of C to form H. Residual parity makes every degree in H even, and w has positive H-degree. The maximal-trail closure argument inside H produces a nonempty closed trail D based at w. Rotate C to start at w and concatenate D with C. Their edge sets are disjoint, so this is a closed trail longer than C, contradicting maximality.

author: high4
claim: Full target solved directly: Let (G) be a finite connected undirected graph with at least one edge. Suppose every vertex of (G) has even degree. Prove that (G) has a closed trail that traverses every edge exactly once.
evidence: Choose a trail T with the maximum possible number of edges. It is nonempty because G has an edge. Write T from v_0 to v_m. If v_0 differs from v_m, then the T-edge incidences at v_m are odd: each nonfinal visit has paired arrival and departure incidences and the final arrival is unpaired. Since the total degree of v_m is even, some incident edge is unused, and appending it makes a longer trail, contradiction. Thus T is closed. Let S be its vertex set. If T omits an edge, connectedness gives an unused edge f incident with S: if an omitted edge has an endpoint in S, use it; otherwise follow a path from S to an endpoint of an omitted edge and take the first edge leaving S, which cannot be a T-edge because every T-edge has both endpoints in S. Let x in S be an endpoint of f. Cyclically rotate the closed trail T to begin and end at an occurrence of x, then append f. This is a trail with one more edge than T because f was unused, again contradicting maximality. Hence T omits no edge. Being a closed trail, it traverses every edge exactly once.

links.attempt_summary: Longest-trail endpoint parity gives closure; connectedness plus cyclic rotation rules out any omitted edge.
